spoken.said: That was paulgsc, in their own voice. What follows is how Rust Rounds works, shown on the phone itself and then explained underneath. First a week as it feels to use it, walked through on the app with sample data for an invented company, Tallowbrook; then, announced when we get there, the internals. It is as of November twenty-fourth, twenty twenty-six, checked against two repositories: some-ui, which holds the app, and server, which holds home, the server on paulgsc's own network. Later commits may have moved things.

spoken.chapter: Chapter one. A week, from Monday to Monday.
spoken.narration: Every Monday at three forty-one in the morning, a routine writes the new week, and it is on the phone when the day starts. It describes a made-up company, a promise its service has to keep, and two to four tickets, each a short Rust program that misses the promise, doesn't compile, or fails only sometimes. This is the week as the phone opens it: Tallowbrook, which prints shipping labels, and what it has to meet.

spoken.chapter: Chapter two. What a ticket asks for.
spoken.narration: Open a ticket, and the program is there with rustc's own words about it: home has already compiled it. Below come the forks, the decisions the ticket asks for. At each, an assistant lists a few options, the way a coding agent would, and marks exactly one as recommended. The recommendation isn't always best, and the best isn't always listed. That is the skill being practised: reading code, and deciding.

spoken.narration: On Monday, an essay answers the week that closed, ticket by ticket, and Studio's Renders shows it coming. It restates each question, plays the answer whole, or says it was silent, and gives a best fit, never called correct, set beside the answer. spoken.chapter: Chapter five. Now the internals: rustc on home.
spoken.narration: Now the internals: if you don't write code, let this part wash over you. Nothing about the compiler is simulated. On home, a service called rust-runner compiles each program with rustc, edition twenty twenty-four, optimisation off, and keeps its errors as JSON, each with its code and the span it points at. Every program is treated as hostile: every compile and run happens under one user kept for programs, never the runner's own, with no network, a read-only root, and caps on memory, processes and time. The program's run gets an empty environment.

spoken.chapter: Chapter six. How home hears a take.
spoken.narration: The owner's voice stays on home, never a cloud service. Home decodes a take with ffmpeg, in a fresh private folder. A voice activity detector, Silero, looks for speech first, because Whisper alone tends to hear thank you in silence; with no speech, Whisper never runs. Otherwise whisper dot cpp, built into home's own server, hears it, and keeps each word's time and how sure it was.

spoken.narration: Monday splits the work on purpose. Code decides what a model needn't: which closed weeks are owed an essay, and a take home couldn't make out never holds one back; and next week's topics, your own pasted errors first, then what has faded, then what no week has touched. Code runs each program and checks both files. Claude writes only the words, from what home heard, never the audio. Home renders the essay: Kokoro speaks as the tutor, and the owner's takes play whole, captioned.

spoken.chapter: Chapter eight. A fork, judged after the deadline.
spoken.narration: Each fork is a deliberation. Every option rests on a model of Rust an engineer could honestly hold, and cites what it trades on: the promise's rows and the ticket's own figures. Only after the deadline does Monday name the best: the recommended one, another, or one nobody listed. The essay places a decision on a scale with five stops, from trusting the recommendation to seeing past the list. Reading the owner's real decision into that scale is next.

params.title: SOLO for each answer, decay across weeks

spoken.chapter: Chapter nine. A published rubric, and decay across weeks.
spoken.narration: Nothing here is a made-up grade. Each answer is read on SOLO, published by Biggs and Collis in nineteen eighty-two and applied to explaining code by Lister and others: five levels, from missing the point to an account carried past the ticket. Knowledge fades, so each concept is rechecked after one, two, four, eight and sixteen weeks. Relational or above moves it up a box; anything less, or silence, sends it back to the first.
